cells.tense: The pen's in your hand right now on this — you decide what the growing thing gets next, and the decision comes from what you actually feel, not from what you owe anyone.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're already growing and do the next small honest thing for it today — the one you'd regret skipping, not the impressive one. Notice what that leaves you with.
cells.core:
On an ordinary day this looks like reading what's in front of you, giving it what it needs, and letting it take its own time after that. You don't wait on a feeling before you act, and you don't rush the pace just to feel like you did something. Both halves are working — seeing what's there and then moving with it.

Where you are, the pull toward one direction is real and it's coming from genuine engagement rather than urgency. What's left to feed is the second yes — staying in the choice after the first easy one, and letting it stay yours once it costs something.
cells.sheetLine: You're deciding what this gets next, and the deciding is yours.
cells.verb: letting a real connection become the direction and moving with it

cells.tense: You're bracing at a version of this that hasn't happened — rehearsing how it could go wrong, deciding what you'll say before anyone has asked, and none of it is the thing in front of you today.
cells.ask: Leave one thing you're growing untouched by your hands for a full day — no checking, no adjusting, no planning ahead about it. See whether it holds without you holding it up.
cells.core:
When this is steady, you match the care to the thing: you see what's actually there, give what it needs that day, and stop. There's a lightness in it even when the work is real, because you're not carrying a future that hasn't arrived. Your hands do less, and the growing thing is fine.

What's changed is the timing, not how much you care. You're doing next month's tending before this one has had its turn, and the energy that belongs to what's growing is going into the picture of it instead. Pushing harder at what's already ahead of schedule doesn't bring it closer.
cells.sheetLine: You're carrying next season before this one has finished.

cells.tense: You're standing at a door that's already behind you — the connection you'd genuinely choose feels like it's in the rearview, and you've stopped acting like you're allowed to want one again.
cells.ask: Tell one person out loud what you want to grow, and let whatever they say land without softening it or taking it back. That's the whole move.
cells.core:
On a normal day when this is working, you notice your own pull toward someone or something and you know it's yours without needing to argue for it. You act like a person who wants a thing and has said so. It doesn't take effort — what you sense lands, and it proves accurate.

What's quiet now is the moving toward it, not the sensing. You can still tell what's real when it's in front of you; you're just not stepping toward it. Saying the want out loud is the smaller, plainer act that pulls the current through — and it's the one the day is asking for.
cells.sheetLine: You can still tell what's real. You've stopped stepping toward it.

cells.tense: The pen is down in a room you're already writing — you shape how this growing thing goes in a hundred small calls, and you describe each one as just how it happened to be.
cells.ask: Name one call you made for this growing thing today — out loud, to yourself — that you've been describing as simply what was needed. Nothing more than the naming.
cells.core:
When this sits right, your care shows in what you do without your announcing it — you adjust, you show up, you make the call, and you're the one making it. Doing and sensing are the same act, and it doesn't need a label to be real. On a good day you can watch yourself make the call and know it came from you.

The shaping is already happening; you're just describing it like it happened to you. The direction is coming from your hand, and saying so is the smaller, earlier thing. That's the piece running without credit — and the one that starts here.
cells.sheetLine: You're making the calls. You've been calling them just how it is.

attempts.check: The record gives the card, seat, status, and medicine, but it doesn't say this person is actually in any specific life situation with a growing thing — the cells have to stay at the level of mechanism and condition, not invent a garden, a project, or a person they're tending. The likeliest objection from a reader is that 'two streams becoming one' sounds mystical or that 'the card' is telling them what's happening; I avoid this by keeping every line at what the capacity is doing, never as a verdict on their history or motives. The asks survive being wrong because they're small, physical, and finishable at the table they're at, and they teach something even if the read is off. The sentence that would serve the writer more than the reader would be anything like 'two streams, one flow' on glass — I'm leaving that out entirely and saying the plain thing.
